title: Revenue per Worker Is Up. Are Firms Getting a Larger Share?
raw_summary: From the Great Recession until 2019, U.S. labor productivity growth disappointed. Nonfarm-business output per hour grew about 1 percent a year from 2010 to 2019, down from 3 percent in the late 1990s. This slowdown was especially pronounced in manufacturing, and it coincided with a slowdown in the growth of revenue per worker among public firms. However, since 2019, growth has picked up to twice the 2010s rate, around 2 percent. In this post, I use data from firms’ 10-K filings to unpack this recent acceleration. I first show that the acceleration appears in public firms’ revenue per worker, then document how the gains went into profit margins, and finally, what firm characteristics predicted significant profit margin increases. The increase in profit margins is consistent with ongoing declines in the labor share of output .

title: Has the AI Boom Impacted the U.S. Current Account?
raw_summary: The AI boom is showing up in different corners of the U.S. economy, including international trade. Imports of semiconductors, servers, and computing equipment have climbed sharply yet the U.S. current account deficit has been largely unchanged. To better understand how the AI boom has not substantially affected the trade balance, consider that the current account is dictated by the gap between domestic saving and investment spending. It turns out that aggregate saving and investment spending have not changed much during the AI boom. Aggregate investment has not risen due to weakness outside the AI sector and business saving has remained robust.

title: Prices, Prices, Prices: Overall Inflation and the Costs You Care About
raw_summary: As fall starts to show itself in cooler weather, I want to discuss a topic that usually raises temperatures: inflation. Like a budget-conscious consumer, the Federal Reserve is highly attuned to changes in the price of goods and services; minimizing such swings is one of the Fed’s primary duties, after all. But how does the Fed’s view of prices differ from that of a consumer? And how does the Fed go about stabilizing prices writ large when it lacks the ability to set prices directly? In this post, I explore that apparent paradox from the perspective of a central banker (though I remain a budget-conscious consumer when off duty).

title: AI Adoption and Employment Expectations: Evidence from a Survey of Small Business Owners
raw_summary: There is little consensus on the effect of AI adoption on employment. Economy-wide measures of pay and headcount have moved little even as AI adoption has spread rapidly, yet narrower measures document declining hiring for workers at the start of their careers or in AI-exposed occupations . In this post, we revisit this topic for U.S. small businesses. We use data from the 2025 Small Business Credit Survey (SBCS) to examine the twelve-month-forward employment and revenue expectations of AI users. We find that firms currently using AI are significantly more likely than non-users to expect increased employment and revenues over the next year, even after accounting for firm and owner characteristics and location. Revenue expectations are most optimistic for AI users that report facing operational challenges in utilizing technology.

title: FEDS Paper: A Macroeconomic Analysis of Household Labor Supply Responses to Large Fiscal Transfers
raw_summary: Isabel Cairó , Shigeru Fujita, and Camilo Morales-Jimenez The fiscal transfers deployed during the COVID-19 pandemic were unprecedented in scale and strongly progressive. Using CPS/ASEC data, we document that the decline in employment during the pandemic was larger for low-income households and tightly linked to the intensity of transfer receipt, a pattern absent during the Global Financial Crisis. We develop and estimate a two-sector, heterogeneous-household general equilibrium model in which low-income households are borrowing-constrained in normal times but can save out of sufficiently large transfers. Because preferences permit wealth effects on labor supply, transfers both reduce labor supply and raise consumption, and a dollar of transfers is split roughly evenly between the two margins. We find that the effects of transfers are state-dependent: because the borrowing constraint binds more tightly in a deeper recession, the same transfer relaxes a tighter constraint and delivers an employment and consumption response about 40 to 50 percent larger during the pandemic than when the same transfer is introduced in the steady state. In the model, transfers were welfare-improving for recipients, with gains diminishing as transfers increase.

title: FEDS Paper: Inattentive Price Setting and Inflation Under Fiscal Policy Uncertainty
raw_summary: Oliver Pfäuti and Edson Wu How do high public debt and fiscal uncertainty interact to shape inflation? We develop a model in which firms face uncertainty about both marginal costs and fiscal policy and choose how much information to acquire before setting prices. Higher debt raises steady-state taxes, affecting attention through two opposing forces. While these taxes reduce the profit stakes of mispricing, they make desired prices more sensitive to tax fluctuations, increasing the value of information. The interaction generates a U-shaped relationship between public debt and attention, and therefore between debt and inflation volatility. Using euro-area firm-level expectations data, we document that the passthrough of expected input-cost growth into expected selling-price growth rises systematically with a country's debt-to-GDP ratio, consistent with the model. In the calibrated general-equilibrium model, an increase in debt from 100% to 175% of GDP raises inflation volatility by about 20%, mainly because firms reallocate attention toward fiscal shocks.

title: Capital One at EMNLP 2026 in Budapest
raw_summary: Capital One researchers and academic partners present 16 accepted papers advancing responsible AI, RAG and LLM evaluation. Advancing natural language processing through multi-sector research Natural language processing (NLP) forms the backbone of modern agentic systems, document intelligence and enterprise artificial intelligence applications. Capital One researchers, in collaboration with our academic partners, are presenting 16 accepted papers at the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026), taking place in Budapest, Hungary, October 24–29. These research papers highlight ongoing investments in foundational AI/ML science, robust red-teaming, graph-encoded retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), intent resolution and trustworthy evaluation techniques. Multi-sector collaboration accelerates the transition of foundational NLP innovations into secure, reliable enterprise systems. By co-authoring several of these papers with university partners including the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, University of Southern California and UNC Chapel Hill, Capital One contributes to open science while addressing complex technical challenges at scale. Highlighted EMNLP 2026 research papers Papers on robustness, red-teaming and model safety: FinRT: Distilling adaptive red-teaming strategies into reusable adversarial generators in consumer finance Rikhiya Ghosh, Himanshu Kumar, Sriram Venkatapathy, Sahil Wadhwa, Alexandre Day, Andy Luo, Pranab Mohanty Large language models remain susceptible to adversarial prompts that induce policy-violating behavior in regulated financial contexts. This work introduces FinRT, a framework that distills adaptive red-teaming strategies into reusable adversarial generators, significantly improving attack detection and safety verification under fixed generation budgets. MEMGUARD: Preventing memory contamination in long-term memory-augmented large language models Hyeonjeong Ha, William Campbell, Yue Wu (academic partnership with University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) Long-term memory integration introduces risks of memory contamination in conversational agents. The authors present MEMGUARD, a defense system designed to inspect, isolate and neutralize untrusted external inputs before they corrupt long-term memory stores. Validity-aware jailbreak evaluation for large language models Qilong Wu, Sahil Wadhwa, Pranab Mohanty, Giri Iyengar (academic partnership with University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) Standard jailbreak evaluations frequently misclassify unviable prompts as successful security breaches. This paper establishes a validity-aware benchmark framework that rigorously validates execution success to ensure accurate safety measurements across frontier language models. Papers on advanced retrieval, graph encoding and intent resolution: CAGE: Coherence-aware graph encoding for retrieval-augmented generation Tong Qi, Jingyu Wu, Youbing Yin, Daben Liu, Erin Babinsky Traditional vector-based retrieval systems often retrieve relevant to query but collectively incoherent text chunks. CAGE introduces a graph-encoding framework that structures retrieved passages into directed heterogeneous graphs to preserve context relevance, factual consistency and cross-chunk coherence. SPARC-RAG: Adaptive sequential–parallel scaling with context management for retrieval-augmented generation Yuxin Yang, Nima Chitsazan, Yash Govilkar, Akasha Tigalappanavara, Sambit Sahu, Shixiong Zhang (academic partnership with University of Southern California) Naive inference-time scaling in RAG causes context contamination and diminishing returns during complex reasoning. SPARC-RAG coordinates sequential refinement and parallel exploration via unified context management, improving accuracy at lower inference cost. Probing ambiguity: Adversarial intent resolution for robust text-to-SQL Youbing Yin, Xujun Peng, Muhammad Uddin, Erin Babinsky, Daben Liu, Anoop Kumar Natural language database queries frequently contain implicit ambiguities that yield multiple SQL query translations. This paper presents Adversarial Intent Resolution (AIR), a multi-agent framework that actively probes for ambiguity, verifies execution differences and generates targeted clarification. The framework remains effective even when only the database schema, not the underlying data is exposed to the LLM. Papers on LLM evaluation, debiasing and benchmarking: The judge can debias itself: Awareness and self debiasing for reliable LLM-as-a-judge Youbing Yin, Jingyu Wu, Anoop Kumar, Scott Novotney, Daben Liu, Erin Babinsky Automated LLM-as-a-judge frameworks inherit systematic biases when evaluating output quality. The researchers introduce new benchmarks for additional bias types and demonstrate that self-debiasing strategies can effectively help detect and calibrate their own biases. T1-Bench: Benchmarking multi-scenario agents in large-scale real-world domains Genta Indra Winata, Amartya Chakraborty, Yuzhen Lin, Swasthi Prasannakumarrao, Shikhhar Siingh, Nadia Bathaee, Sriharsha Hatwar, Houhan Lu, Anmol Jain, Paresh Dashore, Anirban Das, Kshitij Tayal, Xiuzhu Lin, Sambit Sahu, Milind Naphade, Shixiong Zhang Evaluating AI agents across diverse industrial tasks requires benchmarks that reflect operational complexity. T1-Bench offers a standardized, multi-scenario benchmarking environment designed to measure multi-step agent reasoning, tool execution and error recovery in real-world workflows. RECAP: Regression evaluation for continual adaptation of prompts Harsh Deshpande, Kushal Chawla, William Campbell Deploying instruction-following models into dynamic environments exposes them to changing constraints. RECAP measures prompt regression, forgetting and forward transfer when constraint specifications evolve over time, offering new metrics for prompt optimization algorithms. Papers on optimization, vision-grounded agents and software engineering: Beyond the vacuum: Combinatorial strategy selection for competitor-aware generative engine optimization Vaibhav Sourirajan, Yao Zhang, Himanshu Kumar, Sahil Wadhwa, Mann Patel, Amirfarrokh Iranitalab Content rewriting strategies in generative engine optimization often operate in isolation without considering competitive market dynamics. This paper introduces a two-phase optimization pipeline using Bayesian Optimization of Combinatorial Structures (BOCS) and preference optimization to learn optimal content rewriting strategies. A history-aware visually grounded critic for computer use agents Jaewoo Lee, Supriyo Chakraborty, Kartik Balasubramaniam, Sambit Sahu (academic partnership with UNC Chapel Hill) Long-horizon GUI agents struggle recovering from errors. This research introduces a test-time intervention framework HiViG which equips the agent with a goal progress oriented summary to produce better actions. The agent then critiques those actions with visually grounded reasoning to refine them. Across a diverse set of GUI environments , HiViG improves task success rates for open-weight and Gemini-3 Flash models by 5.8% and 9.0% relative to the strongest critics evaluated. AREAs-Lab: An interactive environment for AI-driven requirement elicitation for AI systems Pengshan Cai, Sangwoo Cho, Chenyang Zhu, Kushal Chawla, Scott Novotney, Shixiong Zhang, Sambit Sahu (external collaboration with academic and industry partners) Defining precise software and system requirements for AI implementations remains a manual, error-prone task. AREAs-Lab provides an interactive environment that uses LLM agents to elicit, analyze and refine technical requirements prior to system development. VerTox: Verifiable reward-guided corpus poisoning against neural ranking models Zhiqi Huang, Vivek Datla, Alfy Samuel Neural ranking systems in search architectures are susceptible to corpus manipulation. VerTox establishes a verifiable reward-guided evaluation framework to test neural rankers against sophisticated corpus poisoning vectors. Pin…

title: USC and Capital One announce 2026–2027 AI research awards
raw_summary: Capital One and USC’s Center for Responsible AI and Decision Making in Finance (CREDIF) celebrate 2026–2027 AI research awardees. Advancing responsible AI through multi-sector academic collaboration Capital One selected the 2026–2027 CREDIF Research Award Recipients for joint academic collaborations with the University of Southern California (USC). Established through the Center for Responsible AI and Decision Making in Finance (CREDIF) at USC , these collaborations pair academic faculty with Capital One research scientists to address foundational challenges in machine learning and financial AI systems. Along with these award recipients, two faculty members were chosen to receive our inaugural CREDIF Capital One Faculty Fellowship Award. Granted as a two-year gift to professors spearheading pioneering AI research, these fellowships provide direct support for ongoing research efforts while enabling recipients and their graduate students to actively collaborate with Capital One scientists. The 2026–2027 awarded research collaborations and principal investigators include: Uncertainty quantification for multi-agent LLM systems: Decomposition and failure localization Faculty Lead : Prof. Salman Avestimehr PhD Fellow : Asal Mehradfar Focus : Developing robust frameworks to quantify uncertainty, decompose complex agent workflows and localize failure modes in multi-agent large language model environments. Dynamic schema-guided Monte Carlo for text-to-SQL agents on massive databases Faculty Lead: Prof. Paul Bogdan PhD Fellow: Kien Nguyen Focus: Advancing natural language interfaces for database querying by pairing dynamic schema representation with Monte Carlo search techniques. FinSemKG: A semantic mediation layer for grounded, auditable LLM question answering over financial tables Faculty Lead: Prof. Craig Knoblock PhD Fellow: Md Abrar Jahin Focus: Constructing semantic knowledge graph structures that ensure grounded, explainable and auditable question-answering pipelines for tabular financial data. XFinAgent: Financial analyst agents with sparse-probe control, multi-agent explainability and robust evaluation Faculty Lead: Prof. Mahdi Soltanolkotabi PhD Fellow: Mohammad Shahab Sepehri Focus: Creating autonomous financial analyst agents equipped with sparse-probe mechanistic control, transparent multi-agent interactions and rigorous evaluation benchmarks. Query-adaptive graph traversal and persistent investigation memory for financial knowledge extraction Faculty Lead: Prof. Viktor Prasanna PhD Fellow: Yuxin Yang Focus: Designing adaptive graph neural algorithms and persistent memory representations to execute complex knowledge extraction over relational network data. CREDIF: Multi-signal reward modeling for robust and trustworthy AI Faculty Lead: Prof. Swabha Swayamdipta PhD Fellow: Xinyue Cui Focus: Formulating multi-signal reward mechanisms to align foundation models with complex safety, trustworthiness and operational constraints. The 2026–2027 CREDIF Faculty Fellowship Award Recipients are: Sai Praneeth Karimireddy Research Proposal: Belief-weaver: Probabilistic belief transformers for synergizing language, knowledge and rich feedback PhD Fellow: Zarif Ikram Paria Rashidinejad Research Proposal: Unlocking diverse thinking and planning in AI agents PhD Fellow: Amin Banayeeanzade Bridging academic discovery and real-world application Multisector partnerships give academic researchers direct insight into practical industry challenges while giving Capital One scientists access to cutting-edge theoretical techniques. Each awarded project pairs USC principal investigators directly with Capital One research collaborators to co-develop methodologies, produce open scientific publications and contribute code to the scientific community. Building long-term research opportunities Awarded projects run through the 2026–2027 academic year. Results feed directly into peer-reviewed research papers targeted at academic conferences such as NeurIPS, ICLR and ICML. These initiatives also create career pathways for graduate students through internship programs and professional research roles at Capital One. Congratulations to the CREDIF 2026–2027 awardees! We look forward to a year of discovery and breakthrough innovation born from these multisector collaborations. Originally published at https://capitalone.science . title: Operational excellence in serverless — 5E’s framework
raw_summary: Transform serverless freedom into business agility through the 5E’s framework: empower, engineer, evaluate, evolve and enhance. Modern digital businesses need software systems that are agile, reliable and cost-efficient. At Capital One, we’ve adopted a serverless-first approach to transform how we build and deploy applications, trading server management for a focus on delivering business value. While this paradigm eliminates operational overhead related to infrastructure, it doesn’t eliminate the need for operational excellence. In fact, the distributed, event-driven nature of serverless systems introduces a new set of challenges. When looking to achieve operational excellence in serverless systems, organizations must require disciplined engineering-automation, observability, cost control and a culture of continuous improvement. Understanding operational excellence in the serverless context Operational excellence focuses on how cloud systems are designed, deployed, monitored and optimized for long-term performance and reliability. In a serverless context, it involves: Automation : infrastructure and deployment as code Resilience : designing for failures, timeouts and throttling from day one Observability : collecting logs, metrics and traces across functions and services Cost visibility : paying only for what’s used, while avoiding hidden inefficiencies Continuous improvement : using data and feedback to refine architecture Serverless architecture can reduce reliance on infrastructure management, but it necessitates robust operational discipline to effectively handle distributed workloads. We will now delve into the five guiding principles, known as the 5E’s, which bridge the gap between operational excellence and practical engineering practices. Figure 1: Operational excellence illustrative architecture — The 5E’s Framework for Resilience & Agility Empower: automation and governance Empowerment starts with automation and clarity. Teams must have the freedom to deploy quickly while maintaining consistent operational standards. Engineering practices In practice, this balance is achieved through a core set of engineering practices: Infrastructure as code (IaC) : Use tools such as Terraform, Bicep or CloudFormation to version and review infrastructure changes. Continuous integration/continuous delivery (CI/CD) : Automate builds, tests and rollouts. Integrate static analysis and policy checks early. Policy as code : Apply guardrails for compliance and security directly in pipelines. Self-service deployment : Encourage “You build it, you run it” ownership with automated rollbacks and clear operational visibility. When developers are empowered through automation and safe defaults, organizations gain velocity without sacrificing control. Engineer: reliability, scalability and observability Engineering excellence is the foundation of operational maturity. In serverless environments, systems must be resilient, observable and scalable by design. Reliability patterns These patterns help serverless systems recover gracefully when things inevitably go wrong: Design idempotent functions to handle retries gracefully. Implement dead-letter queues (DLQs) for unprocessed events. Use managed workflow orchestration (e.g., Step Functions, Durable Functions or Workflows) to manage dependencies. Practice fault injection or chaos testing to validate recovery strategies. Scalability and performance These practices keep serverless systems fast and elastic as demand fluctuates: Adopt asynchronous eventing to decouple workloads. Use caching and edge delivery for latency-sensitive paths. Profile cold-start latency and optimize initialization logic. Observability These practices ensure teams can trace, measure and troubleshoot behavior across every function: Collect metrics, logs and traces across all functions. Correlate requests using trace IDs for end-to-end visibility. Build dashboards for throughput, errors and cost per invocation. By engineering observability and reliability into every function, teams can turn runtime behavior into actionable insights. Evaluate: measure what matters Operational excellence is measurable. Success should be based on objective signals, not assumptions. Here are some of the many metrics one might track: These dashboards are made visible within our engineering organization to create shared ownership. When teams track performance and cost together, they discover insights that help them balance agility and efficiency. Evolve: continuous optimization No architecture is ever “done.” Workloads, dependencies and customer expectations evolve, and your systems must evolve with them. Technical optimizations These optimizations keep infrastructure aligned with how the system actually runs, not how it was originally designed: Review usage patterns to tune memory, time-outs and concurrency. Migrate synchronous flows to event-driven designs for elasticity. Automate patching and runtime upgrades through IaC pipelines. Refactor high-cost or underperforming functions using data from cost and performance reports. Process evolution We cultivate an environment where reflection and adjustment happen as routinely as deployment: Schedule quarterly operational reviews focused on metrics, not just code. Introduce internal “learning sprints” where teams analyze incidents and share optimizations. Operational excellence thrives when teams treat every deployment as an opportunity to learn and refine. Enhance: feedback and learning loops The final step is enhancement, turning data into continuous improvement. Operational excellence isn’t static; it’s sustained through learning loops that connect incidents, telemetry and process improvements. Best practices Closing the loop between incidents and improvement comes down to a few key best practices: Conduct blameless postmortems after incidents and feed actions back into code or pipeline rules. Automate alerts for anomaly detection and integrate them with collaboration tools. Align retrospectives around measurable operational KPIs, not just delivery velocity. Reinforce psychological safety. Improvement happens when teams feel safe to surface failures early. Enhancement ensures that excellence becomes a habit, not a one-time achievement. Points to remember Pulling these ideas together, a few key takeaways stand out: Culture and empowerment : Great architecture stems from an empowered team, not just tools. By automating routine workflows, we empower developers to focus on higher-level problem-solving, reinforcing that automation is a partner to human ingenuity, not a replacement. Metrics and customer impact : Use metrics like latency, reliability and cost to gain clarity, always linking them back to how they affect the customer. Visibility and trust: Foster trust by making operational data accessible to everyone. Automation and innovation : Automation frees up time from manual tasks, allowing for greater innovation and improvement. Continuous learning and reliability : Sustain reliability through ongoing evolution of architecture, processes and people. Conclusion Serverless technology frees engineers from infrastructure, but operational excellence transforms that freedom into business agility. It’s not just about scaling code; it’s about scaling learning. By empowering teams with automation, engineering for resilience, evaluating what matters, evolving with data and enhancing through feedback, we’re building cloud systems that are reliable, efficient and continually improving. Operational excellence isn’t a destination-it’s the rhythm of modern serverless architecture. Originally published at https://www.capitalone.com . title: FCA calls on private market firms to manage conflicts of interest in line with rapid growth
raw_summary: Private market firms vary in how well they identify and manage conflicts of interest, according to an FCA review. Private markets refer to investments in assets, companies, or debt not listed or traded on public exchanges. They’ve grown significantly in recent years, and the UK is a leading international centre. Private markets play an increasingly important role in providing capital to businesses and opportunities for returns to investors. Private markets can give rise to conflicts that differ from those in public markets, and effective disclosure is important to enable investors to assess whether their interests are being protected.The FCA found examples of good practice by firms across private equity, private credit and real estate asset classes. These included strong governance arrangements, effective oversight and independent challenge. It also identified some areas where firms could strengthen governance, oversight and conflicts management arrangements to support fair investor outcomes.As private markets grow and business models become more complex, the FCA found that some firms were failing to identify conflicts adequately or keep their controls up to date. Recurring weaknesses were identified in areas including cross-fund transfers and multi-party transactions, gifts and entertainment, and information barriers.The FCA expects firms to be able to identify, record, manage and disclose conflicts effectively, and demonstrate that investors are being treated fairly, particularly in areas where investors place significant reliance on firms' judgement, governance and controls.Michelle Beck, director of wholesale buy-side at the FCA, said: 'Firms need to ensure their management of conflicts of interest keeps pace with growth in their size and complexity. We found good practice across the sector, but standards varied considerably. We want to encourage confidence in the UK’s private markets. Firms should act on our findings and identify where they can strengthen controls.'Although not part of this review, the FCA is examining governance and conflicts concerns relating to the use of private credit to fund consumer litigation claims, including significant risks of harm to investors, consumers and markets.Notes to editorsConflicts of interest and fair customer treatment in private markets.The review examined how firms identify, manage, mitigate and disclose conflicts of interest across private equity, private credit and real estate markets.The report includes examples of both good practice and areas where firms could strengthen arrangements.The review forms part of the FCA's wider supervisory focus on private markets and investor outcomes.

title: Beyond borders: Regulating the risks we share
raw_summary: Speech by Ashley Alder, FCA Chair, at the Michael D. Gill Lecture on International Financial Regulatory Understanding and Cooperation. I wasn’t fortunate enough to work as closely with Mike as many of you in this room.But I knew him well enough during my time with the IOSCO board to appreciate someone who was kind and unassuming, whilst being absolutely determined to make lives better through his work.He personified the very best attributes of dedicated public service.In his 2024 lecture Andrew Bailey described Mike as a passionate internationalist, and reflected on what this meant for the UK after the Brexit referendum.Two years on, the values that Mike championed are even more on point.Mike understood implicitly that relationships between regulators are about so much more than institutional goodwill – they depend on trust, candour and constructive practical action.That’s an aspect of his legacy that is just as relevant – perhaps even more so – today.In an increasingly interconnected global financial system, no institution can see the whole picture on its own.Success depends not only on what each regulator does individually, but on what we can see, understand, test, and address together.

title: FCA restricts 6 firms following concerns over anti-money laundering controls
raw_summary: Restrictions have been placed on 6 unregulated lenders, known as Annex 1 firms, after the FCA raised concerns about their anti-money laundering policies, controls and procedures while assessing their applications. The restrictions were imposed by the FCA on each firm’s request and limit their ability to take on new customers or do new business with existing customers, including extending existing credit.This action forms part of the FCA’s enhanced oversight of Annex 1 firms. These firms operate in sectors that can present a heightened risk of money laundering and other financial crime and are required to register with the FCA for supervision under the Money Laundering Regulations. They are not authorised or subject to wider FCA regulation.The FCA has previously warned Annex 1 firms that they will be subject to increased scrutiny. They must be able to demonstrate they understand the financial crime risks they face and have effective systems and controls in place to manage those risks, or face action.More widely, the FCA is assessing responses to an information request sent to around 900 registered Annex 1 firms to identify and disrupt financial crime risks and determine where further action is needed.The FCA has also reminded regulated firms that, when dealing with Annex 1 firms, they must carry out due diligence to understand the firm’s business, in accordance with legislative requirements. This includes seeking direct confirmation from the firm of its registration status, conducting independent checks of the information it provides, and understanding and managing any risks.Registration under the Money Laundering Regulations is not a substitute for regulated firms carrying out their own appropriate due diligence.Steve Smart, executive director lead for fighting financial crime at the FCA, said: 'We have warned Annex 1 firms that they face increased scrutiny. They must demonstrate they can manage the money laundering risks they face. Where they cannot satisfy us, we will intervene.'Notes to editorsVoluntary restrictions were imposed on Kingscrown Finance Ltd on 21 April 2026, with further voluntary restrictions imposed on 25 September 2026. The further restrictions limit how Kingscrown may receive payments from existing customers and require an orderly wind-down of its existing loan book.On 7 October 2026, voluntary restrictions were imposed on MOMSB Ltd and Momentus Capital Ltd. The restrictions prevent the firms from taking on new customers or entering into new lending arrangements subject to limited exceptions, restrict the circumstances in which they may accept payments from existing customers, and require an independent review of their anti-money laundering framework.On 9 October 2026, voluntary restrictions were imposed on Grosvenor Funding Ltd and Grosvenor Funding (North West) Ltd. The restrictions prevent the firms from taking on new customers or entering into new lending arrangements, restrict the circumstances in which they may accept payments from existing customers, and require an independent review of their anti-money laundering framework.On 15 October 2026, voluntary restrictions were imposed on Abbital Ltd. The restrictions specify the circumstances in which Abbital may take on new customers, enter into new lending arrangements or accept payments from existing customers. They also require an independent review of Abbital’s anti-money laundering systems and controls.Fighting financial crime is one of the FCA's strategic priorities.

title: Reshaping regulation, deliberately
raw_summary: Speech by Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive, at Investment Association Annual Dinner 2026. Reform: more than writing rulesIn this sector, we’re just past peak rule making. The scale of change has been significant – and deliberate.But we’re not done yet.We want to see growth that benefits consumers, supports competitiveness and spurs innovation.Building a stronger retail investment culture takes more than piecemeal rule writing.It takes a strategic approach. One that starts with giving consumers the support they need to make informed financial decisions.And understand both the risks of acting – and the costs of not acting.In that vein, we have reformed our advice and guidance rules.We’ve introduced targeted support.And we’ve moved away from prescriptive disclosures, and placed greater emphasis on outcomes through the Consumer Duty.We want to further support innovation and give firms the confidence to offer more forms of simplified advice at lower cost to consumers.So we’ll soon publish updated rules, alongside case studies we’ve developed with the Financial Ombudsman Service.We’re already seeing real progress.Just 6 months in, more than a dozen firms are already authorised to deliver targeted support.And early signs are promising: consumers who receive it invest up to 53% more than those who don’t.These reforms have taken time and effort – from your teams, and mine.But it’s well worth it.

title: Former chief executive banned after misconduct led to £4m losses in high-risk investments
raw_summary: The FCA has banned Jeffrey Dawkins, the former chief executive of Vector Wealth Ltd, after he dishonestly acted as a front for a disqualified director using the company to sell high-risk bonds. Mr Dawkins has also been fined nearly £270,000.In 2019, Mr Dawkins sold Vector Wealth to a disqualified director who described himself as CEO and wanted to use Vector Wealth’s FCA-authorised status to sell mini-bonds.Mr Dawkins told the FCA he was still in charge, but the new “CEO” was really running the firm. This deception allowed the disqualified director to promote mini-bonds using the legitimacy of the firm to make them appear safer than they were.The disqualified director and Kadir Kanizi, a former senior manager at Vector Wealth, promoted the bonds but investors were not properly warned about the risks.Investors put in £105,000 on average, with one investing £1.1 million. Before seeing the marketing material, they had to confirm they were high net worth or sophisticated investors. Investors are expected to lose about £4 million.The FCA has banned Mr Kanizi from senior management roles. He was fined for failing to make sure consumers were properly warned about the risks.Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said, 'Jeffrey Dawkins acted as a front man for a banned director, helping high-risk investments look safer than they were.'Mr Dawkins and Mr Kanizi allowed misleading promotions to draw in investors, many of whom now face significant losses. Mini-bonds and similar investments are very high risk, and people should be extremely cautious.'The FCA has warned about the risks of investing in mini-bonds and loan notes. A loan note or mini-bond usually involves lending money to a company for a set period in return for interest. If that company fails, consumers could lose every penny.Consumers need to be alert to the risk of harm and protect themselves using the tools available, like the FCA Firm Checker.Notes to editorsRead the final notices for Jeffrey Dawkins and Kadir Kanizi.There is statutory obligation to report the change in control of authorised firms.Vector Wealth Limited was formed as Fifth Quarter Asset Management (UK) Limited on 23 March 2012. Mr Dawkins held authorised positions at the firm from 5 March 2013. Vector Wealth’s authorisation ended on 28 January 2025.Mr Kanizi was appointed as a director on 22 September 2020 and was approved by the FCA on 6 September 2021.The disqualified director was banned from acting as a company director for 12 years in August 2014.The penalty in respect of Mr Dawkins includes a multiplier to reflect the seriousness of the conduct. It also includes an uplift for failing to cooperate with the FCA’s investigation. The full calculation is set out at section 6 of the Final Notice. Mr Dawkins has also been ordered to pay £57,298 plus interest (£68,257) of the proceeds he received from selling Vector Wealth and continuing to act as its director and approved person.The FCA has calculated that Kadir Kanizi should have been fined £80,096 but it reduced the penalty to £20,000 after he demonstrated that it would cause serious financial hardship. In the interest of maximising the funds available to be distributed to investors, the FCA agreed not to enforce the penalty if the same amount was made available by Mr Kanizi to Vector Wealth’s liquidators. He has also agreed to complete consumer duty training before taking up any future role in financial services.Investors who bought bonds through Vector Wealth should contact the firm’s liquidator and check the FCA website for updates.The FCA has investigated the matters that fall within its remit. The FCA may share relevant information with other law enforcement agencies where appropriate. Confirming or comment on individual referrals could risk affecting ongoing investigations.The FCA now actively removes the unutilised permissions of firms. Historically firms were expected to voluntarily request cancellation of unused permissions.The FCA permanently banned the marketing of speculative illiquid securities, including mini-bonds and loan notes, to retail investors from 1 January 2021.Anyone approached about loan notes, mini-bonds or similar high-risk investments should stop and check before investing, especially where adverts promise big, fixed returns or make the investment look simple and safe. Use the FCA’s Firm Checker and Warning List before handing over any money.

title: LIBOR/EURIBOR-related bans

title: Three arrests in major FCA operation against criminal insider dealing ring
raw_summary: The FCA has conducted a major operation to disrupt a suspected organised criminal group for engaging in insider dealing and money laundering. On 13 October, 3 individuals were arrested following a joint operation by the FCA and the National Crime Agency (NCA). More than 100 FCA and NCA staff took part in searches at 5 residential premises in London and Manchester.More than 30 mobile phones, laptops and tablets were seized in searches conducted by FCA investigators.All 3 suspects are in the process of being interviewed by the FCA at police stations in London and Manchester.Steve Smart, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:'Insider dealing is a serious threat to the integrity of our markets. Working with partners, we will continue to use all the powers at our disposal to crack down on serious and organised crime groups engaged in market abuse.'In 2025/26, the FCA secured 4 insider dealing convictions, with 2 resulting in record sentences totalling 11 years of imprisonment. Twelve people were fined a total of £1.77m for insider dealing, market manipulation and making misleading statements.Notes to editorsThe FCA cannot comment further at this time but will provide more details when appropriate.Fighting financial crime is a priority in the FCA’s 5-year strategy.If you have information concerning insider dealing you can contact the FCA by phone on 0800 111 6768 or by using the FCA’s reporting form. Information can be passed confidentially.The FCA enables a fair and thriving financial services market for the good of consumers and the economy. Find out more about the FCA.

title: Two plead guilty after clients lose £2m in fraud case
raw_summary: Two people who worked at financial advice firms have pleaded guilty to fraud after 4 clients lost £2m. Kerry Nelson, the director of Nexus Independent Financial Advisers Limited and Nexus Investment Managers Limited, and Jacqueline Stephens, the firms' business operations manager, admitted all charges brought by the FCA at Portsmouth Crown Court.They admitted defrauding clients between January 2019 and January 2023 and using false documents as part of the fraud. Nelson has also admitted a money laundering offence after money was withdrawn from the firms, which she used to fund her extravagant lifestyle.Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:'This was a serious breach of trust. Nelson and Stephens caused significant losses to clients who relied on them. We will continue to act where people exploit clients for their own gain.'Nelson and Stephens will be sentenced at Portsmouth Crown Court on 10 December 2026. The FCA will seek confiscation proceedings to deprive Kerry Nelson of any financial benefit from her criminal conduct.Notes to editorsThe FCA started criminal proceedings against Kerry Nelson and Jacqueline Stephens in February 2025. For more details see, FCA charges two individuals with multiple fraud charges. They pleaded guilty at Portsmouth Crown Court on 12 October 2026.Fraud by abuse of position is an offence under sections 1 and 4 of the Fraud Act 2006.Using a false instrument is an offence under section 3 of the Forgery and Counterfeiting Act 1981.Converting or transferring criminal property is an offence under section 327(1) of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002.Confiscation proceedings will be pursued under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002.Nexus IFA and Nexus IM were authorised by the FCA. Nexus IFA had permissions to provide investment, mortgage and pension advice and Nexus IM to provide discretionary fund management services. Neither firm was permitted to hold or control client money.On 25 January 2023, the FCA imposed restrictions preventing both firms from carrying on regulated activity and from reducing the value of the assets they held. The High Court placed both firms into administration on 26 January 2023.

title: Motor finance legal challenge to be heard in February 2027
raw_summary: The Upper Tribunal has confirmed it will hear the legal challenges to our motor finance compensation scheme between 16 to 26 February 2027. The scheme was challenged by 3 lenders - Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes Benz Financial Services, and Crédit Agricole Auto Finance - and by Consumer Voice, represented by Courmacs Legal. The scheme is currently partially suspended. However, firms must keep preparing for the scheme and progress complaints as far as possible.Our scheme is the quickest, fairest and most efficient way to compensate consumers and we will defend it robustly.Advice for lenders Lenders must comply with the scheme rules that remain in force. This includes sending letters to some consumers not owed compensation under the scheme.Firms should plan for the possibility that, if the scheme or parts of it are quashed, there may be no motor finance compensation scheme and no complaint handling pause. In that scenario, lenders would need to be operationally and financially ready to resolve complaints through the usual complaint-handling process and within the usual statutory timescales.We expect lenders to plan rigorously for this scenario, make the necessary financial provisions and engage with their auditors.We encourage firms to contact us if they have questions. We will keep our firm web page updated with the latest information.

title: Liam Coleman appointed as chair of the Financial Ombudsman Service
raw_summary: The FCA Board has appointed Liam Coleman as chair of the Financial Ombudsman Service, with the approval of the Treasury. Liam will take up the permanent role on 10 October 2026 for a 3-year term, having served as interim chair for the last year.Ashley Alder, chair of the FCA, commented: 'Liam has brought strong leadership and valuable insight to the Financial Ombudsman Service over the past year. His extensive experience across financial services, regulation and public service organisations will be invaluable as we work together to support a redress system that is fair, predictable and effective for consumers and firms.'Commenting on the appointment, Mr Coleman said: 'I am honoured to take on the permanent role as chair of the Financial Ombudsman Service. It plays a vital role in upholding fairness and trust in the financial system. I am pleased to be able to continue to work with the rest of the Board, the executive team, and our wider stakeholders.'Liam is also group chair of London & Quadrant Housing Trust. He has extensive financial services and public-sector experience, including previous roles at the FCA, NHS Foundation Trust, Nationwide Building Society, Royal Bank of Scotland and Cooperative Bank.Notes to editorsThe FCA is required by the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA) to appoint the chair of the Financial Ombudsman Service, with the appointment being approved by the Treasury.The Board of the Financial Ombudsman Service is responsible for ensuring that the service is properly resourced and able to carry out its work effectively and independently.The Financial Ombudsman Service was set up to resolve complaints between financial businesses and their customers. It can help with most financial services – including banking, insurance, loans, mortgages, pensions and investments. From 1 April 2019, its remit was extended to cover complaints from larger small and medium sized businesses and about claims management companies.The FCA and the Financial Ombudsman Service are working with the government to transform the UK’s redress system and the way in which the Ombudsman operates within it to deliver a service that is consistent, predictable and fair for both firms and consumers, now and in the future.Find out more information about the FCA.Find out more information about the Financial Ombudsman Service.

title: Strong compliance functions support trusted corporate finance markets
raw_summary: Corporate finance firms help businesses raise funding and implement strategic transactions, supporting investment and growth.This brings responsibility: clients need to be able to trust that firms will act with integrity and manage any conflicts of interest. That trust underpins effective wholesale markets activity.In our Regulatory Priorities Report, we said we would assess corporate finance firms’ compliance functions and their ability to challenge the business effectively. We surveyed 411 corporate finance firms about their compliance resources and activities, receiving 382 responses. Although most firms reported carrying out key compliance activities, the findings also show where more needs to be done.There is no single blueprint for what effective compliance looks like. We found that firms operate a range of different practices. But the findings also underline an overarching principle that compliance cannot be seen as simply a series of tasks, but a culture that senior managers must embed throughout the business.

title: New rules to make long-term investment funds clearer
raw_summary: The FCA has set out clearer expectations for asset managers about long-term investments, such as property. This will help give the market more confidence to invest in funds that support private markets.The new rules mean that investors will have to give 90 days' notice to access their funds but will be more certain that they will receive their money.For investors, this means the fund should be clearer from the start about how quickly they can get their money back and whether the fund is right for their needs.Currently some of these funds allow people to take money out daily with no notice period. During periods of stress or volatility there is a risk that some funds may suspend all payments due to lack of available cash. Some are also holding extra cash, leaving less invested in their intended assets.Rushed sales can lower prices, harm investors who stay invested and put pressure on markets.The new notice period would give managers time to sell assets in an orderly way and make liquidity-driven suspensions less likely.Existing funds would have 2 years to comply and give investors at least 1 year’s notice.The proposals bring the UK into line with new international liquidity standards for open ended funds.Michelle Beck, director, markets, at the FCA, said: 'Funds should be clear about whether they offer quick access or are built for longer-term investments like property. Our rules will help firms make that clearer and give the market more confidence to invest.'Notes to editorsRead CP26/35: Fair redemption terms for authorised funds investing in illiquid assets.The FCA is asking for feedback on the proposals by 11 December 2026.The consultation covers authorised fund managers of non-UCITS retail schemes, known as NURS.The FCA uses the term 'inherently illiquid assets' for assets that cannot normally be sold quickly without a significant loss in value. These can include property and infrastructure investments.Fund managers could set a notice period longer than the minimum where the fund’s assets or investment strategy require it.

title: Looking at how we interact with whistleblowers
raw_summary: Just over a week ago, we received the incredibly sad news that a whistleblower, Simon Andriesz, who we had been in contact with over many years, had died. We’ve shared our condolences, and our thoughts are with his family and loved ones.We’re often in contact with people in challenging circumstances.They may be sharing information about a firm we regulate that they’re concerned about, or in the middle of a dispute affecting their financial security.The personal stress of those situations, and dealing with an official body like us, can be – and for many, is – significant.I know the many colleagues who are in contact with whistleblowers and vulnerable individuals always aim to treat them as the people they are – with empathy and professionalism, not simply cases to be managed.That’s vital if people are to feel confident coming to us with their concerns. We’re grateful so many do, with the number of whistleblowing reports increasing 22% last year.To build greater confidence, we’re sharing more information with whistleblowers about the action we take. We provided feedback on each of the 1,252 whistleblowing reports we closed last year. Overall, 42% of these led to direct action to manage or reduce harm. A further 53% informed our wider work and supported harm prevention.We know, though, frustrations remain. Legal restrictions can mean we’re not able to share as much as people understandably want, and sometimes the actions we take don’t meet people’s expectations.None of this means that there aren’t things we could improve.We’ve asked Lea Paterson, who has just joined our Board as an independent non-executive director, to review how we interacted with Mr Andriesz. Lea will look at whether there are things we could have done better, and she’ll help us learn for the future.We must be open and consider if there are ways in which we can improve, especially in how we interact with people who may be particularly vulnerable. I’m grateful to Lea for taking on this important work. We plan to share any lessons she thinks we should learn from, and how we’ll take them forward, early next year.

title: Reforming UK capital markets to ensure they work well for our economy
raw_summary: Speech by Jon Relleen, director of infrastructure and exchanges, at the Reform of the UK Public and Private Capital Markets Summit 2026. The Economic Secretary to the Treasury has discussed the contribution of UK markets to economic growth.I want to build on that by talking about the FCA’s role in reforming capital market rules.The headline is that we've been very busy over the past few years.We’ve now completed major aspects of a multi-year programme of work, to ensure capital markets work well for our economy and support growth.This has already delivered positive changes. But there’s plenty more to come.We are working on further reforms, while also adapting to rapid changes in markets and use of technology.In fact, areas such as tokenisation, AI and markets for trading private company shares have become central to our capital markets policy programme.And that tells us something important. As markets change, our approach has had to change too.The question has not been whether regulation changes. It has been how we adjust in a way that preserves trust while also supporting innovation and growth.Let me start by talking about our approach to the work.We have been working with the Treasury, the Bank of England and in close dialogue with the private sector, on a raft of wholesale market reforms.These draw on formal reports, like the Wholesale Markets Review, our process of reviewing inherited EU regulation, and issues raised by market contacts.Some have suggested the work programme is a list not a strategy. But I think that underestimates it. There are some key principles running through it.

title: Firms’ confidence, satisfaction and trust in the FCA rise
raw_summary: The latest FCA and Practitioner Panel survey shows rising levels of satisfaction, confidence and trust in the FCA among firms, alongside a strong understanding of Consumer Duty expectations. The FCA and Practitioner Panel annual survey of regulated firms provides valuable insights into how firms think we’re performing.The latest survey shows 79% of firms are highly satisfied with their relationship with the FCA, up from 74% last year. The proportion of firms rating the FCA as a highly effective regulator also increased from 69% to 76%, while 75% reported high levels of trust.Firms were most confident in our work to protect consumers (87%), ensure markets work well (85%) and enhance the integrity of the UK financial system (85%). There was a 27-percentage point increase in firms’ understanding of the Secondary International Competitiveness and Growth Objective and a 25-percentage point increase in confidence in our delivery of it.We took on board feedback from last year’s survey and provided further guidance to help firms embed the Consumer Duty. This year, 88% of firms say they understand what we expect on supporting consumers and embedding the Duty.The findings also provide valuable insight into where firms would like to see further progress, including on regulatory burden. We’re already simplifying reporting by removing outdated or duplicated data returns for 90% of firms.Nikhil Rathi, chief executive of the FCA, said: 'A year into our strategy it's encouraging to see growing confidence across many areas of our work. We know there is more to do. For example, while we can’t do our job without the data firms provide, we should continue to simplify requests and make them easier to manage.'Matt Hammerstein, chair of the FCA Practitioner Panel, said: 'This year’s survey results indicate firms continue to have broadly positive views of the FCA, including strong understanding of expectations under the Consumer Duty and significant growth in confidence in the FCA’s ability to deliver on its secondary objectives focused on growth and competitiveness.'The Panel is encouraging the FCA to be clearer about the outcomes it expects its priorities to produce, and more vocal about the progress it is making against these, to strengthen confidence in the UK as a leading global financial centre and attractive place to invest.'In the first year of our strategy, we've delivered an estimated £5.6bn in benefits to consumers and the economy, including launching My FCA, reducing reporting burdens to save firms around £16m annually, and introducing nearly 50 pro-growth measures to boost UK competitiveness and innovation.Since the survey was conducted, we’ve continued our work to deliver landmark reforms, including working with HM Treasury and the Financial Ombudsman Service to modernise the redress framework, support industry delivery of the Advice Guidance Boundary Review, regulating Buy Now Pay Later products, establishing a new regime for cryptoassets, and progressing the PISCES private markets framework.

title: b11847: hip: fix bf16 WMMA operand vector type for gfx11/gfx12 (#30885)
raw_summary: The __builtin_amdgcn_wmma_f32_16x16x16_bf16_w32 (and _gfx12) builtins take their A/B operands as vectors of short (_ExtVector<16, short> / _ExtVector<8, short>), not __bf16. Declaring the fragments as ext_vector_type(N) __bf16 fails to compile: error: cannot initialize a parameter of type 'short attribute ((ext_vector_type(16)))' with an lvalue of type 'const bf16x16_t' (vector of 16 '__bf16' values) short and __bf16 are both 16-bit and the value is only ever passed to the builtin via reinterpret_cast over raw bytes, so changing the element type is bit-identical. The operand type has been short since the builtin was introduced, so this works across LLVM/ROCm versions without a version gate. Fixes HIP builds for RDNA3 (gfx1150/1151) and RDNA4 (gfx1200/1201). Signed-off-by: Pablo Cholaky waltercool@slash.cl

title: Anthropic Adds Opt-In Security Scanning for Critical Open-Source Projects
raw_summary: AI company Anthropic has launched OSS Scanner, a free, opt-in service to find vulnerabilities in open-source projects. Enrolled maintainers receive periodic security reports generated by the company's strongest models, including Claude Mythos. The reports are sent without human review, and project maintainers can choose to validate their findings and decide which proposed fixes to accept. By Matt Saunders

title: Study Finds AI-generated Code Fails to Boost Productivity Due to Downstream Bottlenecks
raw_summary: A recent Harvard study of 718 firms, using the Jellyfish analytics platform, finds that although AI coding assistants and agents increase code volume, this does not translate into a corresponding increase in completed work, partly because AI-generated code increases the workload in later stages of development, particularly code review. By Sergio De Simone

title: Presentation: Actors for Agents: Patterns for Production AI
raw_summary: Manju Rajashekhar explains how the actor model solves the complex runtime challenges of production AI agents. By treating agents as distributed systems, he discusses state ownership, message passing, write-through state, and supervision boundaries to manage failures, continuations, and mutable execution graphs, moving agentic workflows beyond fragile demos to resilient architecture. By Manju Rajashekhar

title: Vercel Labs Open-Sources fx: A Zig Coding Agent Designed to Be Embedded
raw_summary: Vercel Labs has released fx, an experimental open-source coding agent written in Zig. It runs as a CLI, a script component, or an embedded library, including a WebAssembly build. Early feedback questioned its model-agnostic claim and a name conflict with an existing tool. Vercel says the project is pre-1.0 and changing quickly. By Daniel Curtis

title: Article: AI Changes the Data Interface, Not the Query Engine
raw_summary: This article presents a disaster-recovery analytics workflow in which an AI agent generates constrained SQL or Python, DuckDB computes reproducible facts from Parquet, and the agent interprets the results. It explains the determinism split, replayable analysis, and four signals for deciding when an embedded engine is sufficient or a managed lakehouse is justified. By Peihao Yuan

title: Developer Behind the AI-Built Adobe Clones Says They Are “Not Anywhere Close to Ready
raw_summary: A developer used Claude Opus 5.5 to build open-source replacements for seven Adobe applications, promoted them across Reddit with a projection of roughly 100% parity within a month, then told Hacker News the project was not anywhere close to ready. Its own roadmap puts it at 45% ready for real work and 2,300 to 4,100 agent-hours from full parity. By Steef-Jan Wiggers

title: Article Series: Agentic AI Architecture
raw_summary: In this article series, we try to establish agentic AI architecture as a new type of software architecture that will likely dominate the industry for years to come. The articles, written by industry experts, cover various elements and aspects of agentic AI architecture. We aim to present the latest trends and developments shaping the new type of architecture as it enters the mainstream. By Rafał Gancarz

title: Google SynthID Detector Simplifies Watermark Detection and Expands Support to Other AI Providers
raw_summary: Google DeepMind announced the global availability of SynthID Detector, a tool designed to help identify AI-generated content, including media created using AI tools from SynthID partners such as OpenAI, NVIDIA, and Kakao, with Apple support expected soon. By Sergio De Simone

title: TornadoVM 7 Enables GPU-Native Workloads from Java Applications
raw_summary: TornadoVM, an open-source heterogeneous programming framework for Java, has reached version 7.0. It automatically accelerates Java programs on multi-core CPUs and GPUs and provides a rich GPU programming ecosystem in Java that can be used with any mainstream JDK distribution e.g. Temurin, Red Hat OpenJDK, Coretto, Oracle, GraalVM or Zulu. By Ben Evans

title: Presentation: Beyond the Prototype: Scaling Framework Agnostic AI Agent Infrastructure with Ray
raw_summary: The speakers discuss transitioning AI agents from local FastAPI prototypes to resilient production systems on Kubernetes using Ray. They share operational insights on RayCluster topology, stateful memory handling, auto-scaling on dynamic traffic, and robust control plane designs, while highlighting critical guardrails, multi-region setups, and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation pipelines. By Deepak Mohanakumar Chandramouli, Bhumik Vinodkumar Thakkar

title: Article: From Microservices to Agents: the Next Evolution of Distributed Systems
raw_summary: The article examines the transition from microservices to agentic AI architecture in distributed systems. Microservices allow for functional decomposition, while agentic systems focus on decision decomposition. This shift introduces new complexities in observability, reliability, and system design, highlighting the need for updated architectural patterns and practices. By Mallika Rao

title: Podcast: The Future of Web Apps: Will AI Agents Generate UIs on the Fly?
raw_summary: Rachel Lee Nabors, former React core team member, dives into the architecture and philosophy behind local-first applications, exploring how small language models (SLMs) running directly on-device can deliver privacy-focused, low-latency, and cost-effective alternatives to cloud-hosted LLM wrappers. By Rachel Lee Nabors

title: EmbeddingGemma 2 Expands beyond Text to Support Code, Images, Video, and Audio
raw_summary: Based on Gemma 4 and released under the Apache 2.0 license, Google's EmbeddingGemma 2 is a compact, open-weight, multimodal embedding model designed to make semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) more efficient while optimizing performance for on-device deployment. By Sergio De Simone

title: Amazon Acquires DuckLabs and Integrates DuckDB in Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL
raw_summary: Amazon has acquired DuckLabs, the company behind the analytical database DuckDB. Co-founders Hannes Mühleisen and Mark Raasveldt will continue to lead the team under AWS. The acquisition aims to enhance the development and reach of DuckDB while maintaining its open-source status. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL gets its first DuckDB-powered feature following the acquisition. By Gianmarco Nalin
